title: India Reports 29 FDI Investments Worth $511 Million Under Revised Land-Border Rules
excerpt: The investments, spanning IT, AI, pharma, and manufacturing, offer the first evidence that a May policy easing approval requirements for firms with limited Chinese ownership is attracting capital.
body:
• India's commerce ministry reported 29 foreign direct investment proposals worth 48.95 billion rupees ($511.5 million) under a revised automatic route that allows firms with non-controlling Chinese ownership of up to 10% to invest without prior government approval.
  • The investments span information technology, artificial intelligence, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, data centres, and transport services, with investors based in Mauritius, the United States, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, Luxembourg, and the Cayman Islands.
  • The new rules, introduced in May 2026, replaced a blanket screening requirement imposed during the pandemic in 2020 under Press Note 3, which required government approval for any investment linked to a land-bordering country.
  • Direct investment from entities incorporated in China, Hong Kong, or other land-border countries still requires government approval, and majority ownership must remain with Indian citizens or Indian-controlled entities.

First Results of the Policy Shift

India has received 29 foreign direct investment proposals worth 48.95 billion rupees ($511.5 million) under a new automatic route that eases approval requirements for companies with limited ownership ties to land-bordering countries, the commerce and industry ministry said on Friday.

The disclosures are the first concrete indicator that rules introduced in May — which allow investors with non-controlling beneficial ownership of up to 10% from countries sharing a land border with India, primarily China, to invest through the automatic route — are drawing capital. The investments cover information technology, artificial intelligence, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, data centres, and transport services, according to the ministry.

The investors are based in jurisdictions including Mauritius, the United States, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, Luxembourg, and the Cayman Islands, the ministry said. None are direct investments from Chinese entities — the automatic route applies only to third-country firms with minority Chinese ownership stakes.

What Changed in May

In March 2026, the Union Cabinet approved a revision to India's FDI policy for entities with ownership links to land-bordering countries. The rules, notified by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade in May, introduced a clearer definition of beneficial ownership aligned with the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.

Under the revised framework, foreign firms with Chinese beneficial ownership of up to 10% — defined as non-controlling — can invest through the automatic route, subject to sectoral caps and existing regulatory conditions. The policy also created a fast-track approval mechanism for select manufacturing sectors including capital goods, electronic components, and the polysilicon and ingot-wafer value chain, with a 60-day processing timeline.

"It is expected that the new guidelines will provide clarity and ease of doing business in India, and facilitate investments which can contribute towards greater FDI inflows, access to new technologies, domestic value addition, expansion of domestic firms and integration with global supply chain."

— India's Commerce and Industry Ministry

The Press Note 3 Backstory

The original restrictions were introduced in April 2020 through Press Note 3, when India moved to require government approval for any foreign investment where the beneficial owner was from a country sharing a land border — including China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal, Bhutan, and Afghanistan. The policy was widely understood as targeting Chinese investment after fears of opportunistic acquisitions during the pandemic and amid escalating border tensions between the two countries.

But the policy's broad sweep created unintended friction. Global private equity and venture capital funds — including blue-chip firms based in the United States or Europe — found their India investments requiring government screening simply because they had limited partners from land-bordering countries with minority, non-controlling stakes. The ambiguity slowed deal flow and created compliance headaches even for investments with no realistic Chinese influence.

What Stays Restricted

The easing is targeted, not blanket. Direct investment from entities incorporated in China, Hong Kong, or any country sharing a land border with India still requires government approval through the standard route. Investments where beneficial ownership from land-bordering countries exceeds 10%, or where ownership below 10% confers any form of control, also remain subject to prior approval.

Majority ownership and control of investee entities must remain with resident Indian citizens or Indian-controlled entities, even in sectors where the automatic route now applies. All foreign investors must declare their beneficial ownership at the time of investment, and changes in ownership that cross the threshold trigger a fresh approval requirement.

Broader Context

The policy shift comes as India tries to balance two competing pressures: attracting global capital to fuel its manufacturing and technology ambitions, and maintaining strategic guardrails against Chinese economic influence. India's imports from China stood at nearly $132 billion in fiscal year 2025-26, the highest from any single country, underscoring the depth of the economic relationship even as political tensions persist.

"The 29 investments have been reported by investors/entities based in jurisdictions including Mauritius, the United States, the Republic of Korea, Japan, Singapore, Luxembourg and the Cayman Islands."

— India's Commerce and Industry Ministry

For the Indian diaspora in the United States and other countries where several of the investing entities are based, the revised rules remove a practical barrier that had complicated cross-border investment structures. NRI-linked funds and investment vehicles with incidental Chinese limited partner exposure now have a clearer path into Indian markets.
